# Scenario

![Crab_shrimp_coral](../resources/crab_shrimp_coral.jpg){#fig-crabs width="400" height="284"}

To investigate synergistic coral defence by mutualist crustaceans,
@Mckeon-2012-1095 conducted an aquaria experiment in which colonies of a coral
species were placed in a tank along with a predatory sea star and one of four
symbiont combinations:

- no symbiont,
- a crab symbiont
- a shrimp symbiont
- both a crab and shrimp symbiont.

The experiments were conducted in a large octagonal flow-through seawater tank
that was partitioned into eight sections, which thereby permitted two of each of
the four symbiont combinations to be observed concurrently. The tank was left
overnight and in the morning, the presence of feeding scars on each coral colony
was scored as evidence of predation.  The experiments were repeated ten times,
each time with fresh coral colonies, sea stars and symbiont.

The ten experimental times represent blocks (random effects) within which the
symbiont type (fixed effect) are nested.

# Read in the data

```{r readData, results='markdown', eval=TRUE}
mckeon <- read_csv("../data/mckeon.csv", trim_ws = TRUE)

head(mckeon)
#block is random effect
#symbint is within block (random slopes could be an option)
#predation is response (binary so we use Bernouli with logit link function)

#set factor levels and make the control (none) first
mckeon <- mckeon |> 
  mutate(BLOCK = factor(BLOCK),
         SYMBIONT = factor(SYMBIONT, levels = c('none', 'crabs', 'shrimp', 'both')))
```

# Exploratory data analysis

```{r}
#| label: scatterplot
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#symbiont x-axis
#predation y-axis
#facet by blocks

mckeon |> 
  ggplot(aes(y = PREDATION, x = SYMBIONT)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0), shape = 21) +
  facet_wrap(~BLOCK)
  
#might want to consider random slope model because the response is different for different corals
```

::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="50%"}

Random intercepts model formula:
$$
\begin{align}
y_i &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(n, p_i)\\
ln\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_1}\right) &=\boldsymbol{\beta} \bf{X_i} + \boldsymbol{\gamma} \bf{Z_i}\\
\beta_0 &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(0, 2.5)\\
\beta_1 &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(0, 3)\\
\boldsymbol{\gamma_j} &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_b)\\
\sigma^2_b &\sim{} t(3, 0, 1.5)\\
\end{align}
$$

::::
:::: {.column width="50%"}

Random intercept/slope model formula:
$$
\begin{align}
y_i &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(n, p_i)\\
ln\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_1}\right) &=\boldsymbol{\beta} \bf{X_i} + \boldsymbol{\gamma} \bf{Z_i}\\
\beta_0 &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(0, 2)\\
\beta_1 &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(0, 10)\\
\boldsymbol{\gamma_j} &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(0, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})\\
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} &= \boldsymbol{D}({\sigma_b^2})\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{D}({\sigma_b^2})\\
\boldsymbol{\Omega} &\sim{} LKJ(\zeta)\\
\sigma_b^2 &\sim{} \mathcal{t}(3,0,1.5)\\
\end{align}
$$
::::
:::

where $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ and $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ are vectors of the fixed and random effects parameters respectively
and $\bf{X}$ is the model matrix representing the overall intercept and effects of symbionts on the probability of the colony experiencing predation.
$\bf{Z}$ represents a cell means model matrix for the random intercepts associated with individual coral colonies.


# Fit the model

```{r}
#| label: model formula
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

mckeon_form <- bf(PREDATION ~ (1|BLOCK) + SYMBIONT, 
                  family = bernoulli(link = "logit"))

```

```{r}
#| label: get priors
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

get_prior(mckeon_form, data = mckeon)

priors <- prior(normal(0, 2), class = 'Intercept') + #predation for "none" group
  prior(normal(0, 5), class = 'b') + #on logit scale you have a range of -3 to 3 ALWYAS, the mean is 0, and variance you need to be able to move quite a way so needs to be like 3-5
  prior(student_t(3, 0, 2), class='sd') #how variable is the "none" group across blocks?
```

```{r}
#| label: fit model
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

mckeon_brm2 <- brm(mckeon_form,
                 data=mckeon,
                 prior=priors,
                 sample_prior="only",
                 iter=5000,
                 chains=3, cores=3, #one core per chain
                 warmup=1000,
                 thin=5,
                 backend="cmdstanr",
                 refresh=0,
                 seed = 1,
                 control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99))
```

```{r}
#| label: fit model with priors and data
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

mckeon_brm3 <- update(mckeon_brm2, sample_prior = 'yes',
                      refresh = 0)

```

```{r}
#| label: conditional effects
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

mckeon_brm3 |> 
  conditional_effects() |> 
  plot(points = TRUE)

#need to remember these are distributions!!! So mass is not equally distributed along the vertical lines, it is denser in the center by the mean
```

# MCMC sampling diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: model diagnostics again
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

mckeon_brm3 |> 
  SUYR_prior_and_posterior()

mckeon_brm3$fit |> stan_trace(inc_warmup = TRUE)

mckeon_brm3$fit |> stan_ac()

mckeon_brm3$fit |> stan_rhat()

mckeon_brm3$fit |> stan_ess() #ESS is low

mckeon_brm3 |> pp_check(type = 'dens_overlay', ndraws=100)

mckeon.resids <- make_brms_dharma_res(mckeon_brm3, integerResponse = TRUE)
testUniformity(mckeon.resids)
plotResiduals(mckeon.resids, quantreg = FALSE)
testDispersion(mckeon.resids)
```


# Model validation
::: {.panel-tabset}
## brms
:::: {.panel-tabset}
### pp check
Post predictive checks provide additional diagnostics about the fit of the
model.  Specifically, they provide a comparison between predictions drawn from
the model and the observed data used to train the model.


- dens_overlay: plots the density distribution of the observed data (black line)
overlayed on top of 50 density distributions generated from draws from the model
(light blue).  Ideally, the 50 realisations should be roughly consistent with
the observed data.

The model draws appear to be consistent with the observed data.

- error_scatter_avg: this plots the observed values against the average
  residuals. Similar to a residual plot, we do not want to see any patterns in
  this plot.  Note, this is not really that useful for models that involve a
  binomial response


This is not really interpretable

- intervals:  plots the observed data overlayed on top of posterior predictions
associated with each level of the predictor.  Ideally, the observed data should
all fall within the predictive intervals.



The `shinystan` package allows the full suite of MCMC diagnostics and posterior
predictive checks to be accessed via a web interface.


### DHARMa residuals

DHARMa residuals provide very useful diagnostics.  Unfortunately, we cannot
directly use the `simulateResiduals()` function to generate the simulated
residuals.  However, if we are willing to calculate some of the components
yourself, we can still obtain the simulated residuals from the fitted stan model.

We need to supply:

- simulated (predicted) responses associated with each observation.
- observed values
- fitted (predicted) responses (averaged) associated with each observation

**Conclusions:**

- the simulated residuals do not suggest any issues with the residuals
- there is no evidence of a lack of fit.

::::
:::
<!-- END_PRIVATE-->


# Model investigation

```{r}
#| label: make table
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#wanted b_ exponentiated to be on log odds scale, and wanted intercept to be on both probability scale (intercept) and log odds scale (b_Intercept)
mckeon_brm3 |> 
  as_draws_df() |> 
  dplyr::select(matches("^b_.*|^sd_.*")) |> 
  mutate(intercept = b_Intercept) |> 
  mutate(across(matches("^b_.*"), exp), intercept = plogis(intercept)) |> 
  summarise_draws(median, 
                  HDInterval::hdi,
                  rhat, 
                  ess_bulk,
                  Pl = ~mean(.x < 1), #less than 
                  Pg = ~mean(.x > 1)) #greater than

#b_Intercept: The odds of predation are 60x higher than not being predated on in the group with no symbionts. The probability (intercept) of this predation is 98%

#CRABS
(0.04-1) #odds of being predated on when crabs are present declines by 96% (strong evidence)
60.6 * 0.0396 #odds of being predated on when crabs are present = 2.5

#SHRIMP
(0.02-1) #odds of being predated on when shrimp are present declines by 98% (strong evidence)
60.6 * 0.022 #odds of being predated on when shrimp are present = 1.3

#BOTH
(0.007-1) #odds of being predated on when both are present declines by 99% (strong evidence)
60.6 * 0.007 #odds of being predated on when both are present = 0.4

#mean of each group
mckeon_brm3 |> emmeans(~SYMBIONT, type = "response") |> 
  regrid()
```

# Further analyses

```{r}
#| label: contrasts between treatments
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

cmat <- cbind('crab vs shrimp' = c(0, 1, -1, 0),
              'borth vs one' = c(0, -0.5, -0.5, 1),
              'any vs none' = c(-1, 1/3, 1/3, 1/3))
cmat

mckeon_brm3 |> emmeans(~SYMBIONT, type = "response") |> 
  contrast(method = list(SYMBIONT = cmat)) |> 
  tidy_draws() |> 
  exp() |>  #need to undo logit scale
  summarise_draws(median, 
                  HDInterval::hdi,
                  Pl = ~mean(.x < 1), #less than ALG1
                  Pg = ~mean(.x > 1)) #greater than ALG1

#Crab vs shrimp: no strong effect. They are similar.
#Both vs one: strong evidence. Odds decline when you have both.
#any vs none: very strong evidence. Odds of predation decline with any symbiont.

#median > 1, means group 1 prob is greater than group 2
#median < 1, means group 1 prob is less than group 2

#now to get absolute change (percentage)
#the order of the backtransformation (regrid or exp) in relation to contrast matters
#back transformation after contrast is fractional scale
#back transformation before contrast is absolute scale
mckeon_abs <- mckeon_brm3 |> emmeans(~SYMBIONT, type = "response") |> 
  regrid() |> 
  contrast(method = list(SYMBIONT = cmat)) |> 
  tidy_draws() |> 
  summarise_draws(median, 
                  HDInterval::hdi,
                  Pl = ~mean(.x < 0), #less than ALG1
                  Pg = ~mean(.x > 0)) #greater than ALG1

mckeon_abs

#contrast SYMBIONT.crab vs shrimp: probability went up 9 units
#contrast SYMBIONT.borth vs one: probability went down 26 units
#contrast SYMBIONT.any vs none: probability went down 44 units
```

# Further Investigations
## Fit the random intercept and random slope model

```{r}
#| label: random intercept and slope formula
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#1 represents intercept, would usually be (1 + TREATMENT|LEAF)
#TREATMENT|LEAF is a slope for TREATMENT
#its saying intercept and slope are conditional on LEAF (because in the plot we saw different slopes and intercepts for different leaves)
mckeon_form <- bf(PREDATION ~ (SYMBIONT|BLOCK) + SYMBIONT, 
                   family = bernoulli(link = 'logit'))

```

```{r}
#| label: get priors 2
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

get_prior(mckeon_form, data = mckeon)
#need a new prior for "cor" --> correlation between intercept and slope
#but its very simple, the default prior is the only sensible prior (lkj(1))

priors <- priors +
  prior(lkj_corr_cholesky(1), class='cor')

```

```{r}
#| label: model with priors and data 2
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

mckeon_random <- brm(mckeon_form,
                 data = mckeon,
                 prior = priors,
                 sample_prior = 'yes',
                 iter = 5000,
                 warmup = 1000,
                 chains = 3, cores = 3,
                 thin = 5,
                 refresh = 0,
                 backend = "cmdstanr",
                 seed = 1,
                 control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99))

#if you get divergence even after adjusting the delta, then increase warmup
#want divergent transitions < 10

```

```{r}
#| label: compare models 2
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

loo_compare(loo(mckeon_random), loo(mckeon_brm3)) 
#mckeon_random is better than mckeon_brm3 by 2.5 units +- 2 SE.
```

```{r}
#| label: make table 2
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

mckeon_random |> 
  as_draws_df() |> 
  dplyr::select(matches("^b_.*|^sd_.*")) |> 
  mutate(intercept = b_Intercept) |> 
  mutate(across(matches("^b_.*"), exp), intercept = plogis(intercept)) |> 
  summarise_draws(median, 
                  HDInterval::hdi,
                  rhat, 
                  ess_bulk,
                  Pl = ~mean(.x < 1), #less than 
                  Pg = ~mean(.x > 1)) #greater than

#looks similar to mckeon_brm3 except for crabs not having a strong effect now

```

```{r}
#| label: R2 again
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

mckeon_random |> 
  bayes_R2(re.form = NA, summary=FALSE) |> 
  median_hdci()
#y = R^2, 24% of variation in predation can be explained by symbiont (fixed effects only)

mckeon_random |> 
  bayes_R2(re.form = ~ (1|BLOCK), summary=FALSE) |> 
  median_hdci()
#50% explained

#conditional R2 - variation explained by fixed and random effects
mckeon_random |> 
  bayes_R2(re.form = ~SYMBIONT|BLOCK, summary=FALSE) |> 
  median_hdci()
#74% of variation in predation can be explained by symbiont (fixed effects AND random effects with random slope and intercept) --> total amount explained

#26% of variation unexplained
```
